headlines.title: Authorities warn of dangerous surf following rescue at Santa Cruz beach
headlines.description: The viral rescue at a Santa Cruz beach on Saturday served as a powerful reminder of why experts say people should swim only at beaches with lifeguards on duty. Thursday night, many headed to Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz. They were having bonfires and others were watching the sunset. Santa Cruz is known for its beautiful beaches, but officials say conditions can change in an instant. “Sometimes you’ll go down to the beach, and you won’t see any waves for a period of time and a whole set will come in,” said State Parks Peace Office Micah Moore. “It’s easy to kind of get lulled into oh this is a tranquil day at the beach not realizing that in the next 5, 10 minutes there may be some pretty big surf.” Santa Cruz 17 hours ago Santa Cruz Jul 29 Santa Cruz Jul 28 Those were the conditions last weekend when 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams rescued a 10-year-old boy from the dangerous surf at Seabright Beach. California State Parks says the boy was swept about 15 yards into the ocean before Williams reached him. The 10-year-old was identified as Nathaniel Rai by his father, Sumit Rai, who says he couldn’t believe Williams fought the powerful current to save his son. “And for him to have to grab my son who weighs about 100 pounds when he’s lost consciousness and is limp. Basically deadweight that he’s carrying through those rip currents to bring back to shore is incredibly courageous, brave, heroic. You know he just demonstrated so much resilience and persistence. He never let go of him,” Sumit Rai said. The rescue has been viewed millions of times across the country and even caught the attention of President Donald Trump, who has invited Williams to the White House.

headlines.title: San Bruno neighbors say Waymos have left people traveling to SFO on their street
headlines.description: Residents in San Bruno’s Belle Air Park say they are frustrated that Waymo autonomous vehicles have recently been dropping off passengers headed to San Francisco International Airport in their residential neighborhood. San Bruno city officials have received these complaints from neighbors and are in touch with Waymo to discuss possible solutions. In particular, residents said these Waymo vehicles have been heading to the 500 block of Seventh Avenue, which is the residential street city leaders say is closest to SFO. Neighbors said they began noticing this uptick in Waymo vehicles here about two weeks ago, and the frequency escalated. Six neighbors spoke with NBC Bay Area about their experiences, citing repeated instances of passengers dropped off by Waymos, holding their luggage on the street and looking confused. “One of the gentlemen was trying to go to, I think he said Switzerland,” said neighbor Robert Riechel, who has lived in the neighborhood for twenty years. Riechel said he has spoken with several of these stranded passengers. “And either they’ve got to call somebody else, or one gentleman I talked to had 3 rolling suitcases, he said, ‘I’m gonna walk,'” Riechel recalled. Riechel estimated that would require at least a 20-minute walk down busy San Bruno Avenue. In terms of driving distance, this neighborhood is about 3 miles or ten minutes from the SFO terminals. Neighbors also said the Waymos have been stalling or parking in their neighborhoods for extended periods of time, blocking resident driveways. “This afternoon, two houses up, there was a Waymo parked across the driveway, and the young lady in the house, she wanted to get out, and we tried to holler at the machine or whatever and tell em’ ‘You’re blocking the driveway!'” Riechel recalled. One neighbor said she counted 29 Waymos in the neighborhood on Sunday. On Thursday, neighbors counted five. San Bruno City Council Member Marty Medina, who represents the neighborhood, explained that he and other city leaders have been in touch with Waymo via email about these neighborhood concerns and are working to coordinate a phone call. “In my email to them, I was explaining just how impacted this area is for parking and how inconvenient it is for passengers to get dropped off here,” Medina said. Medina noted this neighborhood has a history of being impacted by airport traffic and parking. Residents have had issues with people parking their cars on the streets and then heading to the airport for a long trip. Street parking is in short supply, and last year the police department asked residents to stop using cones or garbage cans to reserve street parking spots. Medina noted that because of issues with cabs and limosines parking on city streets, the city enacted an ordinance barring vehicles for hire from parking on residential streets. When it comes to the Waymos in the street, Medina is optimistic relief will be on the way for residents soon. “We’ll find a solution, hopefully Waymo and others are willing to work with us,” Medina said, adding that perhaps something could be worked out to have Waymo park in vacant city parking spots instead. San Bruno Police confirmed that their officers had been called to the neighborhood twice to address Waymo-related issues, and that on Thursday one of their officers spoke with a Waymo representative who was on the street. Thursday evening, a Waymo spokesperson responded to NBC Bay Area with a statement saying, “Thanks to the rider’s in-app feedback and outreach to rider support, we were able to remedy the situation.” The statement continued, “We’re committed to learning from these moments and making the rider experience as seamless as possible. Neighbors said they will be watching to see what happens next. Waymo began a limited service to SFO in January of this year. A Waymo spokesperson explained that all Waymo passengers now have the capability to get rides to SFO and to be dropped off at either the Grand Hyatt or at the SFO Rental Car location. However, those locations require a trip on the SFO Air Train to reach the terminal. This is different from San Jose Mineta International Airport, where Waymo vehicles are able to drop passengers off right across from the terminal.

headlines.title: Prosecutors reveal new details ahead of trial involving former Oakland mayor
headlines.description: Federal prosecutors are revealing new allegations in what they’re calling a pay to play scheme involving former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao, her boyfriend and owners of California Waste Solutions. This comes just months before the trial is set to begin. Ahead of an October federal corruption trial, prosecutors are revealing new details they say show an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao, her partner Andre Jones and California Waste Solutions Executives David and Andy Duong. “This is reading like a true crime novel not a traditional pay to play bribe scheme,” Legal analyst and attorney Steven Clark said. The most shocking details center around a 2023 Vietnam trip. Prosecutors say Thao became angry and worried about her political future after learning a reporter was asking about alleged drug use and activity involving prostitutes by former San Leandro Councilmember Bryan Azevedo while on the trip. Court filings claim the Duongs later paid a reporter’s associate $10,000 to stop the story from being published. “The jury is going to have a very different picture of the former mayor when they hear about this information and that she was associated with these individuals and continued to associate with them even after some of this evidence came to light,” Clark said. Azevedo has pleaded guilty to conspiracy in a separate case and is expected to testify at Thao’s trial. Prosecutors also allege Thao shared sensitive city council information with Andy Duong and falsified records of a $150,000 job for jones to secure their home lease. Additionally, they claim jones received $95,000, just part of the $300,000 he received in return for providing Duongs with city contracts. Clark says the new details only helps the prosecution if it’s allowed into evidence. “The conspiracy allegation is very helpful to the government’s case. It gives them an opportunity to bring any type of information that explains the relationship of the parties and also they are going to argue this is in furtherance of a conspiracy to commit this bribery,” he said. Prosecutors also claim andy duong secretly recorded politicians in compromising situations for possible political leverage. His attorney says he was not charged in relation to the new allegations saying in part: “the motion does not concede the veracity or characterization of the government’s allegations at issue, which will be contested at trial. “They were trying to gather evidence to hold over peoples’ heads in this case in case and use it against them if things went wrong but now that evidence, they gathered it is going to be used against them, and it really backfired. That is going to be very difficult for them to explain,” Clark said. The new allegations are part of a fight over what evidence jurors will be allowed to hear. The defense argues much of it is unrelated to the charges. A federal judge has not yet ruled ahead of the October trial. Thao, Jones, and David and Andy Duong have all pleaded not guilty. NBC Bay Area requested comment from all the defendants, but only heard back from Andy Doung’s attorney.

headlines.title: ‘We're cooked': Bay Area college students struggle to find affordable housing
headlines.description: College students are gearing up to head back to campus, but for many in the Bay Area, finding a place to live has become a significant challenge. San Jose State University continues to be a popular college with increasing enrollment every year. It’s also in the heart of Silicon Valley, one of the most expensive places to live in the country. “It feels like ‘The Hunger Games,’” San Jose State student Kyla Jimenez said. “That’s the best way I can describe it.” Kyla is a business major at San Jose State. Her twin Ren is studying communications at nearby Santa Clara University. They can’t find an affordable place to live in downtown San Jose. “We’ll kind of be in competition with families and other people that are just looking for housing as well,” Kyla said. “We’re also in competition with people that are looking in groups of like five or they’re willing to offer more than the asking price.” Kyla and Ren aren’t alone. Several other students expressed the same anxiety. Making It in the Bay 12 hours ago San Francisco Jul 29 Kyla and Ren’s mom is a single parent in Fairfield, so the twins rely on financial aid to pay tuition and housing. “We’ve been touring a lot of two-bedrooms, a lot of three-bedrooms, and a lot of them are just super filthy, like disgusting almost,” Ren said. “A lot of mold is painted over.” On-campus housing is not an option for Kyla. It costs about $9,000 to $10,000 a semester at the campus village, with a meal plan. San Jose State said that price is actually not too bad. “We know this is an expensive housing market,” San Jose State spokesperson Michelle Smith McDonald said. “We are providing one of the best values in downtown in terms of all the things that students get in residential housing.” For a family with little income, the twins said they’re forced to look elsewhere. “It’s just super uncertain,” Kyla said. “I feel like the only word to describe it is cooked. I feel like we’re cooked. We’ve been looking since March.” Ren said they’ve been on edge as they constantly search for a place. “On our phones, on our laptops, checking our emails every day seeing if landlords are even considering our application,” she said. “A lot of it is just disappointment after disappointment.”

headlines.title: Santa Cruz beach rescue could lead to lifeguards getting first responder status
headlines.description: The dramatic rescue at Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz beach could lead to all lifeguards getting official recognition as first responders. Kudos and appreciation have been coming in waves for the young lifeguards who rescued a 10-year-old boy from the dangerous surf in Santa Cruz over the weekend. A 16-year old lifeguard was first to go into the water, and he’s getting big thanks from the rescued boy’s family. The video of the rescue is dramatic, and intense and it’s being seen all over the country. The 10-year-old boy, now identified by his father as Nathaniel Rai, got knocked off his feet and became unconscious as he was pulled into the powerful surf. The father, Sumit Rai, says he couldn’t believe 16-year-old State Parks rookie lifeguard Ryder Williams battled the powerful current even going under himself several times. “And for him to have to grab my son who weighs about 100 pounds when he’s lost consciousness and is limp, basically deadweight that he’s carrying through those rip currents to bring back to shore is incredibly courageous, brave, heroic. You know he just demonstrated so much resilience and persistence. He never let go of him,” he said. The rescue comes as state legislators review a proposed bill that would make lifeguards, officially, first responders. Some people like Melissa Olivo and Scott Seixas, who are still in awe of the rescue, couldn’t believe lifeguards aren’t considered first responders already. “I think it’s important that we recognize them as first responders because of the bravery and the dedication of what they do, the mentality,” Olivo said. “Yes, it does surprise me. Like, if an EMT, a nurse, other people like that who are in, kind of, the life-saving business are first responders. That did surprise me,” Seixas said. Analysts say giving lifeguards first responder status would bring them more professional recognition, support and resources, and could offer them better worker protections and benefits. Santa Cruz State Senator John Laird, who will ultimately be voting on that proposed bill, says the designation is not that simple. “Of course, lifeguards are first responders, but first, first responders also go through this rigorous training, so you’d have to decide because in the peace officer standards training you go through eight months of training, so you’d have to decide what’s appropriate here: how does it work? How does it get designated? What training comes with it? Who pays for it?” he said. Laird says he anticipates the bill will probably not be addressed until next year because of all the bills that still need to be voted on this year.

headlines.title: Have shoppers gotten used to paying more amid rising prices?
headlines.description: Despite a strong overall economy, consumers’ money is not going as far as it used to. With inflation still a tick above 3%, it’s been steady lately, but thanks, largely, to energy costs, it’s still higher than expected. That being said, after cutting back, many consumers tell us they’re back to shopping, traveling, and spending, because they have to. The latest numbers from the Commerce Department show prices and spending are still rising. Business Professor Caroline Chen says we’ve gotten used to paying more so we’re shopping through it. “I think people are in a state of tolerance at this point, because you have put off for so long buying the thing you’ve been saving for, and yes, it’s more expensive that what you hoped it would be, but then you’re tired of waiting, so you buy it at the elevated price,” she said. Scott Budman has more in the video report above.

headlines.title: Wildfire in Sonoma County triggers Spare the Air Alert and evacuations
headlines.description: The smoke from the wildfire that broke out along the coast of Sonoma County Thursday has affected the air quality in the North Bay, prompting a Spare the Air Alert. The wind-driven Woodside Fire burning near Salt Point State Park has scorched at least 75 acres in heavy timber and was 20% contained, according to Cal Fire. Evacuation orders were issued for zone SON-1D1, Salt Point State Park, Steelwater Cove Regional Park, Ocean Cove Private Camp, and the Timber Cove Subdivision, according to Cal Fire. An evacuation warning was issued for zone SON-1D2. Highway 1 was shut down between Stewarts Point-Skaggs Springs Road and Timber Cove Road, officials said. The smoke of the fire has impacted the air quality in the North Bay, leading to a Spare the Air Alert being issued. Authorities said the alert will be in effect until Friday and added wood burning is banned. “High levels of particulate matter pollution are harmful to breathe, especially for children, seniors and those with respiratory and heart conditions,” officials said. “Avoid smoke exposure by staying indoors, if heat is not an issue. If temperatures are too high indoors, visit a Clean Air Center or other facility with filtered air.” The Sonoma County Health Officer issued the following health advisory: “Areas of Sonoma County may experience ‘very unhealthy’ or ‘hazardous’ air quality caused by the wildfire event along the coast near Timber Cove and Salt Point State Park. People may experience adverse health effects from the smoke over Sonoma County and across the region.” This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: San Francisco opens its first Jollibee after a 6-year delay
headlines.description: A new Jollibee restaurant will open in San Francisco tomorrow, six years after its announcement. The restaurant faced many challenges that slowed down its initial opening, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Mayor Daniel Lurie joined a few devoted citizens and other officials to celebrate the soft opening on Market Street. He also discussed his administrations effort to streamline permitting and other bureocratic obstacles that harm businesses. “It’s unacceptable that it took six years. And it’s why from day one we’ve been trying to slash the red tape, cut the bureaucracy, get more permits online. 80% of permits right now are done in 30 days or less. Many of them can be done online,” Mayor Lurie said. The union representing city IT workers raised red flags about what they allege are security holes in the permitting software that was created by a San Francisco-based tech company called OpenGov. But last month, the city’s Civil Service Commission allowed the lucrative contract to remain. Supervisor Danny Sauter, the new representative of the district where the restaurant now is, says the permitting process used to be a labyrinth of departments. “This was, believe it or not, a historic district. And so, there was almost a year of going back and forth between the business and city departments to understand, is this in the district, is it not? What does that actually mean? And that’s a clear example of; we can’t put up with that nonsense in the figure,” he said. Beginning tomorrow, devoted Jollibee fans will finally get to enjoy the restaurant’s signature fried chicken and spaghetti.

headlines.title: Bay Area residents more likely to own homes after leaving region, study finds
headlines.description: Many Bay Area residents who leave the region are finding a more affordable path to homeownership, but often at the cost of lower incomes, lower-performing schools and greater climate risk, according to a new report released Thursday by a University of California research institute. The study by California Policy Lab found that people who move out of the Bay Area typically relocate to neighborhoods where home values are about 50% lower, and rents are about one-third cheaper than where they lived before. Residents who leave California are also 33% more likely to own a home five years after moving. Researchers said they analyzed anonymized consumer credit data to track Bay Area households over time, examining who leaves, where they move, and how their finances and neighborhoods change after relocating. Housing remains the Bay Area’s biggest financial challenge, according to the report. Nearly 40% of residents — including nearly half of renters — spend more than 30% of their income on housing. The median Bay Area home cost about $1.4 million in early 2026, compared with $915,000 statewide and $425,000 nationally. “The Bay Area continues to offer tremendous economic opportunity, but it’s also the most expensive metro in the country,” California Policy Lab executive director Evan White said in a statement. “Our research shows many residents are achieving affordable homeownership elsewhere, but often at the cost of lower incomes, lower-performing schools, or greater climate risk.” According to the report, Bay Area residents who move elsewhere in California or out of state generally end up in neighborhoods with lower average incomes and, for those remaining in California, schools with lower standardized test proficiency. Those leaving the region also tend to move to areas with that are more vulnerable to climate-related hazards such as wildfires, flooding and extreme heat. Researchers also found that residents leaving the Bay Area are not necessarily coming from its wealthiest or poorest neighborhoods. Instead, they generally leave neighborhoods that reflect the region overall but are, on average, in weaker financial shape than their neighbors, with credit scores 23 points lower and more than twice as much student debt. Migration is also changing the region’s demographics. White residents are leaving the Bay Area on net, while residents of color — particularly Asian and Pacific Islander households — are moving into the region in greater numbers or leaving at lower rates, making the Bay Area more racially diverse overall, researchers said. California Policy Lab researcher Brett Fischer said the findings raise broader questions about who can afford to live in the Bay Area as housing costs remain high and demand could increase further. “Our research strongly suggests that high housing prices are pushing people out, a trend that some fear may be exacerbated by the AI boom putting more pressure on housing prices,” Fischer said. Earlier this month, Gov. Gavin Newsom was in Oakland when he signed legislation aimed at lowering the cost of building affordable housing in California. The measure is expected to reduce construction costs by an estimated $60,000 to $70,000 per affordable housing unit by streamlining financing and reducing fees, while also extending state homelessness funding and creating a disaster rebuilding fund. Newsom lamented about how the state has historically not supported affordable housing. “We designed a system, a machine, over the course of the last half century to make it more difficult to build. It was intentionally designed, it wasn’t by chance, it wasn’t by happenstance. It was designed not to build. And that requires not just to think differently and argue for different results, but to rebuild the mission,” he said.

headlines.title: Power issue at BART's Pittsburg/Bay Point station causes delays
headlines.description: A PG&E power issue at BART’s Pittsburg/Bay Point station is causing delays for trains Thursday afternoon, according to the transit agency. BART initially reported the problem at about 1:45 p.m. and shortly after 2 p.m. said the power issue was causing delays of 20 minutes in both directions on the Antioch line. There is no estimate yet for when regular service will resume.

headlines.title: 1 injured after car crashes into San Jose business
headlines.description: Police are investigating after a vehicle crashed into a building in San Jose. The incident was reported at 11:39 p.m. in the 1700 block of Story Road, police said. Aerial coverage from NBC Bay Area’s SkyRanger showed half of a vehicle into the front of the Crawfish Bros business. Police said a person was taken to a hospital with non-life threatening injuries following the collision. The driver also remained on scene and is cooperating with the police investigation. No other information was immediately available. San Jose Jul 29 San Jose Jul 29 San Jose Jul 29 Bicyclist injured following crash involving vehicle in San Jose

headlines.title: Randy's Donuts to open first Bay Area location – right next to a local favorite
headlines.description: Randy’s Donuts, a Los Angeles-based chain, is set to open its first Bay Area location in Santa Clara. Randy’s will open up shop at 2595 Homestead Rd. – right across the street from Stan’s Donut Shop, a local favorite since 1959. The grand opening of Randy’s is set for 7 a.m. Friday. The first 25 customers will get free doughnuts and swag from the owners. After that, all customers who arrive before 12 p.m. will receive a free glazed raised doughnut. Randy’s is known for its lengthy menu, which includes raised, buttermilk and premium doughnuts.
